patterns.name: comment.block.carve
patterns.comment: A %%% fence line is a delimiter plus an insignificant tail (spec PART 9 section 28): only the leading run of % is structural, so `%%% TODO` opens and `%%% end` closes. %%% carries no info string - a raw passthrough block is a CODE fence with an =FORMAT info string - so `%%% html` is a comment. The end backreference matches the opener width exactly, so %%%% nests %%%.

A DELIMITED INLINE COMMENT, `{% ... %}` (spec PART 9 section 21a, markup-carve/carve#1239). It hides its payload the way `%%` hides the rest of a line, so it is scoped WHOLE rather than letting the emphasis and attribute rules reach inside - `{% *not bold* %}` must not render a bold run. It sits after the code and literal inline rules so a `{%` inside a code span stays code, and before #trailing-comment so a `%%` in the payload does not open a second comment. IT MAY SPAN A LINE BREAK, and this was a single-line `match`, so a comment written across one was not recognized at all and the markup inside it coloured: `a {% *b*` over ` %} z` scoped a strong run inside a comment - carve#1239 again, one line further on. 144 of 469 generated documents leaked (markup-carve/carve-grammars#320). Prism and highlight.js were given the multi-line reading in markup-carve/carve-grammars#312. The region carries the scope and offers no patterns, so everything between the delimiters is comment. A BLANK LINE ENDS IT, which is the bound Prism uses for this construct too. A TextMate begin sees one line and cannot look ahead for its own closer, so without a bound an unclosed opener would scope the rest of the document. One paragraph is where the engine stops reading this construct as well.
patterns.name: comment.block.inline.carve

patterns.comment:
A HEADING IS STILL A HEADING BEHIND A CONTAINER PREFIX (`- # h`, `- [x] # h`, `> # h`, and `- x` over ` # h`), and `#headings` cannot reach any of them: it is a single `match` anchored on a column-0 run of hashes, and the container's own begin match has already consumed `- ` or `> ` by the time the line is scanned, so the heading carried NO heading scope at all (markup-carve/vscode-carve#131). Corpus 363-a-task-item-s-checkbox-is-not-decided-by-its-first-block renders `- [x] # h` as an `

` inside the item. The gap had been measured into three separate `tests/categories.json` skip reasons before it was ever filed, because the `no scope lives only in a skipped category` gate is structurally unable to report an ABSENT rule: a rule that emits no scope can never be an orphan. That is the same blindness that let the missing hard break survive every green run until markup-carve/vscode-carve#119. TWO BRANCHES, and both are needed. The \\G branch is the marker line, anchored the way `#block-quote-on-marker-line` and `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` are: \\G matches at the current scan position, which on a marker line is exactly where the marker ended, vscode-textmate resets it on every following line so this can never open one there, and the `(?<=[ \\t])` guard keeps it to a marker rather than to a hash run glued after some earlier match on the same line (carve-js renders `- /a/ # h` as item text, not as a heading). The `^[ \\t]+` branch is the container's own body column, where a heading is equally invisible today: carve-js renders `- x` over ` # h` as an `

` inside the item and this grammar scoped it as nothing. REACHABLE ONLY FROM `#container-body` AND `#block-quote-body`, never from the document level, because at the document level an indented hash run is NOT a heading: carve-js renders ` # h` as `

# h

`. Inside a container the indent cannot be counted against the content column from here, so an OVER-indented hash run (`- x`, a blank line, then ` # h`, which carve-js renders as a paragraph) is scoped as a heading. That is the same over-coloring trade-off `#thematic-break` already takes with its `^\\s*`, taken here only inside containers rather than at the document level too. The quoted spelling behind an ALTERNATING prefix (` > # h`) is deliberately still out of reach: the quote's begin consumes one space only, and accepting the rest of the run would scope `> # h` as a heading where carve-js renders `

# h

`.
patterns.name: markup.heading.carve

patterns.comment: A CODE FENCE IS A CODE FENCE BEHIND A CONTAINER PREFIX TOO (`- ```` ` on an item's marker line, and a fence at the item's own body column), and `#code-blocks` could reach neither: its begin is anchored on a COLUMN-0 run of backticks or tildes, with no indent allowance and no marker-line variant (markup-carve/vscode-carve#128). The consequence was worse than a missing colour. Because no block region opened, the fence BODY was tokenized as live markup, so emphasis, links and reference definitions inside a code block all lit up, and the closing fence carried no scope either. corpus 361-a-paragraph-opened-after-a-block-in-an-item-is-still-open-for-a-lazy-line-3 renders `- ```` ` over `  c` over `  ```` ` as a `<pre><code>` inside the item. THE MARKER-LINE RULE HAS TWO BEGIN BRANCHES. The \\G branch is the marker line, anchored the way `#block-quote-on-marker-line` and `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` are: \\G matches at the current scan position, which on a marker line is where the marker ended, vscode-textmate resets it on every following line so this can never open one there, and the `(?<=[ \\t])` guard keeps it to a marker rather than to a backtick run glued after some earlier match on the line. The second branch matches a NESTED marker line WHOLE, for the reason `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` gives: an unclosed fence opened at a nested marker would otherwise swallow its own sibling, because a container boundary written as a column-0 line is one a nested marker never reaches. Capture 1 is the opener's indent, and vscode-textmate splices an unset capture as the empty string, so on the \\G branch `^(?![ \\t]*$)(?!\\1[ \\t])` degrades to that column-0 boundary. The blank-line guard is load-bearing: an item spans blank lines and so does a fence inside it, so without it the first blank line inside the block would end it and the real closer would be read as an opener. A fence at the container's own BODY column is the SEPARATE rule below, and it is separate because it needs a different boundary: its body sits AT the opener's indent rather than past it, so `^(?!\\1[ \\t])` would close it on its own first body line. REACHABLE ONLY FROM `#container-body`, never from the document level, because at the document level an indented fence is NOT a fence: carve-js renders `  ```` ` over `  code` over `  ```` ` as a paragraph holding an inline code span, and the `indented-code-fence-is-not-a-fence` shapes in tests/block-battery.test.mjs pin that. THE END HAS TWO BRANCHES for the reason `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` gives. The first is the ordinary closer, INDENTED because the closer sits at the container's content column; it is deliberately as loose about the fence character and width as the document-level rule beside it, which also closes a backtick fence on a tilde line. The second is a zero-width container boundary: a column-0 line ends the item and with it an unclosed fence. Without it an unclosed indented fence would run to end of document, and vscode-textmate does not test an enclosing container's `end` while a child region is open, so the item could not stop it. NOT included in `#block-quote-body`: `#block-quotes` ends at `$`, so a multi-line region opened inside it would hold the quote open past its own end and run away. A fence inside a quote is therefore still uncoloured, tracked separately.
patterns.name: markup.raw.block.fenced.code.carve

patterns.comment: A CODE FENCE AT A CONTAINER'S OWN BODY COLUMN, the other half of markup-carve/vscode-carve#128 and the reason it is a separate rule from the marker-line one above rather than a third branch of it: THE BOUNDARY IS DIFFERENT. A fence opened on a marker line has its body PAST the opener's indent, so `^(?!\\1[ \\t])` bounds it; a fence opened at the body column has its body AT the opener's indent, so the same test would close it on its own first body line. Here the boundary is `^(?!\\1)`, a line that does not even reach the opener's indent, with the same blank-line guard - a code block may hold blank lines, and an item spans them. carve-js renders an indented fence over an indented body over an indented closer as a code block inside the item. REACHABLE ONLY FROM `#container-body`: at the document level an indented fence is not a fence at all, which the `an indented fence at the document level is not a fence` assertion pins.
patterns.name: markup.raw.block.fenced.code.carve
markup.other.figure-group.carve
patterns.comment: COMPOSITE FIGURE (PART 9 S4c, markup-carve/carve#1215; ported from markup-carve/carve-grammars#223, tracked by markup-carve/carve-grammars#222). The kind word `figure` is reserved among the `:::` types: a BARE opener - the fence, its separator, the word `figure`, and NOTHING else - is ONE figure of ordered panels, not an admonition, so it carries its own scope and this pattern sits BEFORE the generic div pattern below. THE WHOLE DISTINCTION IS THE TAIL of one line: an opener carrying a quoted title or a `[label]` (`::: figure "T"`, `::: figure [g]`) is not that production at all, does not match here, and falls through to the div pattern - which is the generic Tier-2 container the clause says it stays, with title and label preserved. THE SEPARATOR IS A SPACE RUN, NEVER A TAB (grammar.ebnf PART 7, MARKER SEPARATORS; corpus 254): `:::<TAB>figure` renders as a paragraph, so it is spelled ` +` rather than the `\s*` the div pattern beside it uses - a tab-separated opener falls to that pattern and reads exactly as it does today, an over-colouring this rule neither widens nor fixes. Trailing whitespace after the kind word is insignificant and may be a tab. THE GROUP CAPTION NEEDS NO RULE: it is an ordinary `^ ` line one line below the closing fence, which the caption pattern under `#tables` already claims at document level and inside every container body. The optional bullet prefix is carried over from the div pattern, because a group may open directly after a list marker (`- ::: figure`) just as an admonition may. RESIDUAL, written down rather than left to be rediscovered: GROUPS DO NOT NEST - a bare `::: figure` at any depth inside an open group is a generic container - but a `:::` opener here is a per-line `match` with no region, so this grammar has no notion of being inside one and over-colours the inner opener as a group too. carve-grammars carries that rule through a begin/end pair; restructuring the div pattern into begin/end is what it would take here as well, and is deliberately not part of this change.

patterns.name: markup.other.div.carve
patterns.comment: A div fence may open directly after a list marker (`- ::: note`), so an optional bullet prefix is consumed here and scoped as a list marker. A BARE `::: figure` opener never reaches this pattern: it is a composite figure, not a generic container, and the pattern above claims it first (PART 9 S4c). An opener carrying a title or a `[label]` does reach it, which is the point of the split. THE SEPARATOR BEFORE EVERY TOKEN IS A SPACE RUN, never a tab and never nothing: the engines read `:::note`, `:::<TAB>note`, `:::|` and `::: note<TAB>"T"` as paragraph text (corpus 254 and 255), and this rule used `\s*` at every slot, so it coloured all of them as openers. A tab belongs at the start of a line and nowhere else on one. The ONE slot that takes no separator is the bare `[label]`: `:::[l]` does open a div, measured, so that branch alone is zero-or-more spaces. Trailing whitespace after a complete opener stays permissive, tab included, which is what the engines accept - and the line is now anchored, because an unanchored match let a trailing token run claim residue the opener had already been decided against.

table-row-cells.comment: The cells of a table ROW, shared by `#tables` and `#table-row-behind-a-container-prefix` so the two cannot drift apart - the same reason `#container-body` and `#block-quote-body` exist. The two rules differ only in their anchor: one opens at the line start, the other at the scan position on a container's own marker line.

patterns.comment: GFM delimiter/alignment row: a whole line of only pipes, dashes, optional alignment colons, and whitespace (e.g. `|---|---|`, `|:---:|`). Gated by a full-row lookahead so an ordinary data cell that merely contains dashes is NOT mis-scoped. Each dash/colon cell is the separator; the pipes keep their separator scope. Note: TextMate rules are line-local and do not track table position, so a dash/colon-only row that is NOT the parser's second-row delimiter (e.g. a body row that happens to be all dashes) is also highlighted here. That edge case is rare and cosmetic; modeling exact delimiter-row position would require a full multi-line table state machine.
patterns.name: markup.table.row.separator.carve

patterns.comment: Separator cell: leading/trailing alignment colons get a dedicated alignment scope; the dash run stays the separator punctuation.

The continuation row (`+ b |`), which folds into the row above it. INDENT-TOLERANT for the same reason the row rule beside it is: a table inside a list item sits at the item's content column, and a column-0 anchor here left `  + b |` unscoped under a `  | a |` that did scope (markup-carve/vscode-carve#129). It inherits that rule's known over-match at the document level, where carve-js renders an indented pipe row as a paragraph.
patterns.name: markup.table.continuation.carve

patterns.comment:
CAPTION. THE MARKER SEPARATOR IS A RUN, AND NONE OF IT IS CONTENT (PART 7 MARKER SEPARATOR, markup-carve/carve#1583). The separator gets its own capture and the content capture may not start with a space, so `^ cap` captions `cap` rather than ` cap`. The `(?![ \t]*$)` guard is what makes a marker with NOTHING after its run a paragraph instead of a caption: on `^ ` the old ` +(.+)$` let ` +` give one space back so `(.+)` could match it, scoping a caption whose content was a single space, while carve-js renders `

^

`. The guard is the same one `#headings` carries for the same reason - the two constructs share the rule and had drifted apart on it. A TAB IS NOT PART OF THE SEPARATOR, so `^ \tsecond` captions `\tsecond` with the tab kept, which is why the content capture excludes a space rather than all whitespace.
patterns.name: markup.table.caption.carve

patterns.comment: A CAPTION IS STILL A CAPTION BEHIND A CONTAINER PREFIX (`> ^ cap`), and the caption rule in `#tables` cannot reach it: that rule is anchored on `^[ \t]*`, which tolerates indentation but not a marker, and the quote's own begin match has already consumed `> ` by the time the line is scanned - so the caption carried NO caption scope at all. Corpus 405-a-quote-holding-a-captioned-block-indents-it-like-any-other-nested-block renders `> ![a](i.png)` over `> ^ cap` as a figure inside the quote. `#block-quote-body` already reaches headings, thematic breaks, table rows, fences and reference definitions this way; the caption was the construct left out, and an ABSENT rule is exactly what the coverage gate cannot report, because a rule that emits no scope can never be an orphan (the blindness `#headings-behind-a-container-prefix` was filed for). Anchored on \G with the `(?<=[ \t])` guard for the reasons `#table-row-behind-a-container-prefix` gives. Reachable ONLY from `#block-quote-body`: containers reach the caption through `#tables`, whose `^[ \t]*` anchor already matches at a container's own body column.
patterns.name: markup.table.caption.carve

patterns.comment: A TABLE ROW MAY OPEN ON A CONTAINER'S OWN MARKER LINE (`- | a |`, `- [ ] | a |`, `1. | a |`), and `#tables` cannot reach it: its begin is `^(?=\\s*\\|)`, which tolerates indentation but not a marker, and the container's own begin match has already consumed `- ` by the time the line is scanned, so the row carried no table scope at all while carve-js renders a table inside the item (markup-carve/vscode-carve#129, corpus 361-a-paragraph-opened-after-a-block-in-an-item-is-still-open-for-a-lazy-line-2). Quotes (`#block-quote-on-marker-line`) and divs (the optional marker alternative in `#divs`) both already had a marker-line path; tables did not. Anchored on \\G with the `(?<=[ \\t])` guard for the reasons `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` gives: \\G matches at the current scan position, which on a marker line is where the marker ended, vscode-textmate resets it on every following line so this can never open one there, and the guard keeps it to a marker rather than to a pipe glued after some earlier match. The begin is ZERO-WIDTH so the cells rule owns every character of the row, exactly as it does at the line start. Reachable ONLY from `#container-body`. The DELIMITER-row spelling on a marker line is deliberately not duplicated: it cannot arise, because a GFM delimiter row is the second line of its table and a marker line is the first.
patterns.name: markup.table.row.carve

patterns.comment: A lone `+` at the marker column is the list-continuation marker, not a bullet (`+` is never a bullet in Carve).
patterns.name: markup.list.continuation.carve

patterns.comment: A LIST ITEM IS A CONTAINER, NOT A LINE (markup-carve/vscode-carve#61, ported from markup-carve/carve-grammars#94). It opens on its marker line, stays open across blank lines, and closes on the first nonblank line indented BELOW its content column - the marker's ACTUAL width, `indent + marker + separator`, not a fixed two columns. That is what tells an indented definition apart from a below-column one: `- a` over `  [r]: /u` keeps its definition, while `- - a` over ` [^f]: x` sits below every open content column and is item TEXT that defines nothing (corpus a-definition-below-every-content-column-folds-as-text, markup-carve/carve#624). A TASK ITEM'S CONTENT COLUMN IS TWO PAST THE INDENT WHATEVER THE SEPARATOR IS - the checkbox absorbs the rest, so it gets its own branch ahead of the plain bullet rather than inheriting the marker-width test. Measured, not assumed: carve-php and carve-js agree that a body line two columns in belongs to the item for every separator width from one space to five, where the same widths under a plain bullet carry the column with them (`-   a` puts its body at column 4, `-   [x] a` keeps it at column 2). The checkbox glued to an attribute block (`-{.c} [x] done`) is still not scoped - the known limitation this branch inherits, not one it adds.

A LIST ITEM IS A CONTAINER, NOT A LINE (markup-carve/vscode-carve#61, ported from markup-carve/carve-grammars#94). It opens on its marker line, stays open across blank lines, and closes on the first nonblank line indented BELOW its content column - the marker's ACTUAL width, `indent + marker + separator`, not a fixed two columns. That is what tells an indented definition apart from a below-column one: `- a` over `  [r]: /u` keeps its definition, while `- - a` over ` [^f]: x` sits below every open content column and is item TEXT that defines nothing (corpus a-definition-below-every-content-column-folds-as-text, markup-carve/carve#624). THE TEST IS EXACT FOR A BULLET at any indent and any separator width: a bullet marker is one column and the separator is captured whitespace, so `\1[ \t]\3` reconstructs the column count from the marker line itself. A TAB counts as one column here rather than advancing to the next tab stop, and a continuation line has to repeat the marker line's own indent characters. A marker line may carry several markers (`- - A` opens two nested lists), so scope each one, not only the line-anchored first. A BULLET MAY BE GLUED TO AN ATTRIBUTE BLOCK, and then the required space comes after the block, not after the marker - so `-{#x} item` and `*{.c} item` went uncoloured on a line that IS a list item, while the ordered rule beside it already had the branch (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126). It is a LOOKAHEAD: consuming the block would make this rule own those characters, so the attribute rule could no longer scope them. KNOWN LIMITATION, shared with every Carve TextMate grammar: the checkbox after a glued block (`-{.c} [x] done`) is not scoped, because the task branch has none; the bullet is. THE PAYLOAD MUST BE VALID, not merely brace-delimited: an invalid one means the `{` is literal content and the line is prose. `-{+a+} text` (corpus 90-list-item-attributes-6) and `1.{2=v} text` are paragraphs, while `-{} item` and `-{not attrs} item` are list items. Identifiers are STRICT (PART 9 S14) and admit no colon, which is what carve-js does (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126).

The attribute-glued bullet (`-{#x} item`). Its content column cannot be counted, because the block's width is not whitespace, so this branch uses the MINIMUM content column, indent plus two: the container stays open across a range an exact test would have closed, which is the over-coloring side every block rule in this grammar already takes. A marker line may carry several markers (`- - A` opens two nested lists), so scope each one, not only the line-anchored first. A BULLET MAY BE GLUED TO AN ATTRIBUTE BLOCK, and then the required space comes after the block, not after the marker - so `-{#x} item` and `*{.c} item` went uncoloured on a line that IS a list item, while the ordered rule beside it already had the branch (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126). It is a LOOKAHEAD: consuming the block would make this rule own those characters, so the attribute rule could no longer scope them. KNOWN LIMITATION, shared with every Carve TextMate grammar: the checkbox after a glued block (`-{.c} [x] done`) is not scoped, because the task branch has none; the bullet is. THE PAYLOAD MUST BE VALID, not merely brace-delimited: an invalid one means the `{` is literal content and the line is prose. `-{+a+} text` (corpus 90-list-item-attributes-6) and `1.{2=v} text` are paragraphs, while `-{} item` and `-{not attrs} item` are list items. Identifiers are STRICT (PART 9 S14) and admit no colon, which is what carve-js does (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126).

A LIST ITEM IS A CONTAINER, NOT A LINE (markup-carve/vscode-carve#61, ported from markup-carve/carve-grammars#94). It opens on its marker line, stays open across blank lines, and closes on the first nonblank line indented BELOW its content column - the marker's ACTUAL width, `indent + marker + separator`, not a fixed two columns. That is what tells an indented definition apart from a below-column one: `- a` over `  [r]: /u` keeps its definition, while `- - a` over ` [^f]: x` sits below every open content column and is item TEXT that defines nothing (corpus a-definition-below-every-content-column-folds-as-text, markup-carve/carve#624). AN ORDERED MARKER IS NOT ONE COLUMN WIDE, and Oniguruma cannot count the width of a captured run - vscode-textmate splices a begin capture into the `end` pattern as literal TEXT, so a backreference reproduces the marker's characters, never its length. The width is therefore spelled out: one branch per marker width, each consuming exactly that many characters and asking its `end` for exactly that many columns. EXACT for widths 1 to 5 (`.`, `1.`, `10.`, `iii.`, `1000.`), which covers every ordered marker in the corpus; the width-5 branch also accepts anything wider and under-counts it, holding the container open a column or two too long rather than closing it early. Ordered markers use a trailing `.` or `)` only. A parenthesized `(1)` / `(a)` form is NOT a marker in Carve (it is too easily confused with prose), so no leading `(`. The BARE DOT is a marker on its own (carve#472): `.` continues an ordered sequence, and is the only marker allowed to drop its value. The lookahead admits a marker glued to an attribute block (`.{#x}`, `3.{#k v}`), which is how the corpus writes it - but the ATTRIBUTE FORM NEEDS CONTENT TOO: `1.{#x}` with nothing after the block is a paragraph, so the glued-block branch spells the block out in full rather than skipping it. A `\{[^}]*\}` run stops in the wrong place, because a quoted value may contain `}` and may escape its own quote, and `{title="a}b"} x` is a valid item (markup-carve/carve-grammars#85). A ROMAN RUN IS CASE-CONSISTENT: two classes, not one `[ivxlcdmIVXLCDM]`, which matched any mixture and coloured `Vim. text` and `Mix. text` as lists where carve-js renders paragraphs (markup-carve/carve-grammars#118). `mix.`, `civil.` and `did.` DO open lists, so the fix is the case split rather than rejecting multi-letter words. THE PAYLOAD MUST BE VALID, not merely brace-delimited: an invalid one means the `{` is literal content and the line is prose. `-{+a+} text` (corpus 90-list-item-attributes-6) and `1.{2=v} text` are paragraphs, while `-{} item` and `-{not attrs} item` are list items. Identifiers are STRICT (PART 9 S14) and admit no colon, which is what carve-js does (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126).
Ordered marker, width 2. See the width-1 branch above for why the widths are spelled out one branch at a time.
Ordered marker, width 3. See the width-1 branch above for why the widths are spelled out one branch at a time.
Ordered marker, width 4. See the width-1 branch above for why the widths are spelled out one branch at a time.
Ordered marker, width 5. See the width-1 branch above for why the widths are spelled out one branch at a time.

The attribute-glued ordered marker (`1.{#x} item`, `.{#x} item`), on the minimum content column for the same reason the glued bullet branch is: a block width is not whitespace and cannot be counted. Ordered markers use a trailing `.` or `)` only. A parenthesized `(1)` / `(a)` form is NOT a marker in Carve (it is too easily confused with prose), so no leading `(`. The BARE DOT is a marker on its own (carve#472): `.` continues an ordered sequence, and is the only marker allowed to drop its value. The lookahead admits a marker glued to an attribute block (`.{#x}`, `3.{#k v}`), which is how the corpus writes it - but the ATTRIBUTE FORM NEEDS CONTENT TOO: `1.{#x}` with nothing after the block is a paragraph, so the glued-block branch spells the block out in full rather than skipping it. A `\{[^}]*\}` run stops in the wrong place, because a quoted value may contain `}` and may escape its own quote, and `{title="a}b"} x` is a valid item (markup-carve/carve-grammars#85). A ROMAN RUN IS CASE-CONSISTENT: two classes, not one `[ivxlcdmIVXLCDM]`, which matched any mixture and coloured `Vim. text` and `Mix. text` as lists where carve-js renders paragraphs (markup-carve/carve-grammars#118). `mix.`, `civil.` and `did.` DO open lists, so the fix is the case split rather than rejecting multi-letter words. THE PAYLOAD MUST BE VALID, not merely brace-delimited: an invalid one means the `{` is literal content and the line is prose. `-{+a+} text` (corpus 90-list-item-attributes-6) and `1.{2=v} text` are paragraphs, while `-{} item` and `-{not attrs} item` are list items. Identifiers are STRICT (PART 9 S14) and admit no colon, which is what carve-js does (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126).

Definition-list TERM line: a leading `::` marker. Only the marker is scoped (mirroring the single-colon definition rule below), so a trailing `%% comment` and any inline markup in the term still tokenize normally. Matched before the single-colon rule; `::` never collides with a `:::+` fenced div, which needs three colons.
patterns.name: markup.list.definition.term.carve

patterns.comment: Definition-list DEFINITION line: a single `:` marker followed by the definition body.
patterns.name: markup.list.definition.carve

patterns.comment: A FOOTNOTE definition, and until markup-carve/carve-grammars#307 every scope on it said LINK REFERENCE DEFINITION. The rule is right - it is anchored on `[^label]:` and it is the one definition shape that opens a container - but it was copied from the link definition below and kept that construct's names, so `[^a]: note text` scoped the whole line `meta.link.reference.definition.carve` and put `markup.underline.link.carve` on `note`, the first WORD of the prose, as though it were a URL. A footnote body is inline content and has no destination, so that capture carries no scope at all now. The construct ledger read this row as a GAP the whole time, because the only name the rule had was another construct's. A FOOTNOTE definition has a BODY, and that body's content column is a FIXED two whatever the label is wide, so it is the one definition shape that opens a container: `[^a]: note` over `  [r]: /u` collects the second definition (corpus a-definition-on-a-footnote-body-s-continuation-line-is-collected), one column in leaves it the document's own text, and three or more is the body's own text. Narrowing the definition rule below to flush-left without this would have dropped the scope from that shape entirely. A LINK reference definition gets no container, deliberately: it has no body at all, so an indented definition under one is a paragraph, not a second definition (measured against carve-php and carve-js - `[r]: /u` over `  [s]: /v` renders the second line as prose). `begin` consumes exactly what the definition rule below consumes and carries the same captures, so a footnote definition line tokenizes as it always did. Capture 0 carries the old rule-level `name`, which a begin/end rule cannot carry itself - a rule-level name spans the whole REGION, so the body lines would be scoped as definition too. A capture-0 name does NOT reach a sibling capture that re-tokenizes with its own patterns (vscode-textmate builds that sub-tokenization from the RULE stack, not from the capture's local stack), so the attribute capture names the scope itself or a trailing `{...}` block silently loses its definition layer. The trailing group captures an optional `{...}` attribute block using the same strict-identifier body #attributes validates, and recurses into #attributes so the block gets meta.link.reference.definition.carve (this rule's own name) layered with meta.attributes.carve and the entity captures - not only the sibling meta.attributes.carve it already got from the independent root #attributes pattern. Those attributes reach every link resolving the label (markup-carve/carve#612), so they are meaningful content, not decoration (markup-carve/vscode-carve#67).

FLUSH-LEFT: an indented definition at document level is prose, not a definition (corpus indented-reference-and-footnote-definitions-stay-literal). Indented spellings are reached through `#definitions-in-container`, which only a container's body can see, so the column question is answered by the container that opened rather than by this line on its own. The trailing group captures an optional `{...}` attribute block using the same strict-identifier body #attributes validates, and recurses into #attributes so the block gets meta.link.reference.definition.carve (this rule's own name) layered with meta.attributes.carve and the entity captures - not only the sibling meta.attributes.carve it already got from the independent root #attributes pattern. Those attributes reach every link resolving the label (markup-carve/carve#612), so they are meaningful content, not decoration (markup-carve/vscode-carve#67).
patterns.name: meta.link.reference.definition.carve

patterns.comment: An abbreviation definition is recognized only at document level (markup-carve/carve#611), unlike a link/footnote reference definition, which a container also collects. So this pattern is anchored at literal column 0 - no leading whitespace - while the reference-definition pattern above stays column-agnostic. Indenting `*[HTML]: ...` inside a list item, block quote, or any other container makes it inert prose, not a definition (markup-carve/vscode-carve#65).
patterns.name: meta.abbreviation.definition.carve

patterns.comment: A quoted title may contain escaped characters (`"ti\"tle"`), so the title run must consume `\\.` pairs instead of stopping at the first backslash - otherwise the whole link loses its scoping.
patterns.name: meta.link.inline.carve
meta.span.inline.carve
patterns.comment: THE BRACE RUN HAS TO BE A REAL ATTRIBUTE BLOCK. The lookahead was `(?={)`, which asked only that a brace follow - so `[a]{xlink:href=u}` scoped as a span while every engine renders the whole line as literal text, because an attribute name admits no colon (spec markup-carve/carve#870, corpus `an-attribute-name-admits-no-colon`). It now looks ahead for the same block the `attributes` rule matches, including the empty `{}` form that is valid only glued to a preceding `]`.
Same escaped-title handling as the inline link: consume `\\.` pairs inside the quoted title.
patterns.name: meta.image.inline.carve

patterns.comment: THE OTHER TWO IMAGE SPELLINGS. The spec gives an image the same three forms a link has (grammar.ebnf `reference_image`, `collapsed_reference_image`) and says only the leading `!` and the `` output differ. This file had a rule for the inline form alone, so `![alt][ref]` and `![alt][]` fell through to `meta.link.reference.carve`, which matches from the `[` and leaves the `!` as prose - the alt text carrying a LINK title scope. That is worse than leaving them unscoped: the output says the document holds a link where it holds an image. It wins over the reference-link rule without reordering the pattern list, because it matches one character earlier and vscode-textmate takes the leftmost match. ONE RULE FOR BOTH FORMS: the label body is starred, so the collapsed spelling is this rule with an empty label - the fold vim-carve and sublime-carve make for the link (markup-carve/carve-grammars#318), and the one `meta.link.reference.carve` beside it already makes. The label may not span a line (corpus 352-a-bracketed-construct-s-identifiers-stay-on-one-line-3), and the alt text may be EMPTY, so it carries no non-empty guard: `![][r]` is an image where `[][r]` is not a link.
patterns.name: meta.image.reference.carve

patterns.comment: Inline footnote `^[content]` (core Carve). Its content is inline-parsed (spec `inline_footnote = '^[', inline_content, ']'`), so nested emphasis and code still tokenize. The `(?=$)` alternative in `end` bounds the span to one line so an unclosed `^[` cannot leak into following paragraphs. The `(?![ \t]*\])` guard keeps the opener from firing on an EMPTY note: `inline_content` is not optional, so `x ^[]` and `x ^[ ]` are literal text and `x ^[]{.c}` is a literal caret followed by a SPAN, yet all three used to highlight as a footnote (corpus an-empty-inline-note-is-literal).
patterns.name: meta.footnote.inline.carve

patterns.comment: Consume a backslash escape before the `end` check so `^[a \] b]` does not terminate at the escaped bracket.
patterns.name: constant.character.escape.carve

citations.comment: Citation group: a bracket whose content contains at least one @key and has no (url)/[ref]/{attrs} tail. A leading + signals an integral/in-text citation. Items are ;-separated; each may carry a -/+ prefix and an optional , locator. The @key and the -/+ per-item markers are scoped distinctly, analogous to @mention but inside the citation bracket.

patterns.name: markup.citation.carve
patterns.comment: Match the whole citation bracket [+?...@key...]  that is NOT followed by (, [, or { (which would make it a link, ref-link, or span). A lookahead for @ inside the brackets discriminates from plain spans and footnote refs.
Optional -/+ per-item modifier immediately before the @key
patterns.name: keyword.operator.citation.modifier.carve

patterns.comment: @key: citation key with allowed charset [A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_:.#$%&+?<>~/-]*
patterns.name: variable.other.citation.key.carve

patterns.comment: Semicolon item separator
patterns.name: punctuation.separator.citation.carve

code-callouts.comment: CodeCallout markers: <N> where N is one or more digits. Leading form at the start of a callout annotation line (^<N> prose); trailing form inside fenced-code body lines (code  <N>). Both share the same scope.

patterns.comment: Leading callout annotation line: <N> at the very start (with optional leading whitespace), followed by a space and annotation prose.
patterns.name: markup.callout.annotation.carve

patterns.comment: Trailing callout marker inside a code line: <N> at the end of the line (optionally preceded by whitespace).
patterns.name: markup.callout.marker.carve

patterns.comment: An empty attribute block is valid only glued to a preceding `]` (`[x]{}` -> x, corpus 66); a bare `{}` in prose is literal text (corpus 123).
patterns.name: meta.attributes.carve

patterns.comment: Strict identifier (spec PART 9 S14): a class/id/key may not start with a digit, so `{2=v}` stays literal text instead of scoping as an attribute block. An unquoted value may contain dots and colons (`{k=v.w}`); a quoted value may contain an escaped quote (`{title="a\"b"}`); a bare `{}` stays literal.
patterns.name: meta.attributes.carve
entity.other.attribute-name.carve
patterns.comment: No colon. The enclosing match already forbids one, so this could never paint a colon-bearing name and the two only disagreed on paper - but a reader checking the rule found the permissive spelling first (spec markup-carve/carve#870).

An unquoted value may contain dots and colons (k=v.w); consume it whole so the dot is not mistaken for a class. The lookbehind carries the KEY as well as the `=`, because a sub-pattern's lookbehind reads the whole line and not just the captured attribute block: a bare `(?<==)` also fired on an `=` sitting immediately BEFORE the opening brace, so a table cell whose attributes follow the header-kind marker (`|={.total}`) matched `{.total` as one unquoted value and lost the class scope. `|{.total}`, `|>{.num}` and `|=<{.h}` all scoped correctly, which is why it read as a table defect rather than an attribute one. A key always ends in an identifier character, so requiring one cannot exclude a real `key=value`.
patterns.name: string.unquoted.attribute.carve

patterns.comment: AN UNPARTNERED RUN IS A CODE SPAN TO THE END OF ITS PARAGRAPH, which is what the engine does with it and what Prism was taught in markup-carve/carve-grammars#312. Without this rule the run was not a code span at all here, so `a `*b*` coloured a strong inside a verbatim payload - 75 of 111 generated documents, and 37 of 73 on a wide run (markup-carve/carve-grammars#320). Second in this context, so a run that finds its partner is still the closed span above; this one only sees the runs that rule cannot match. A BLANK LINE ENDS IT: the paragraph is where the engine stops the span, and a TextMate begin has no way to look ahead for a closer it already knows is not there. IT ALSO CLOSES ON A MATCHING RUN, which is what makes it the MULTI-LINE code span as well as the unpartnered one: the rule above is a `match` and a TextMate match sees one line, so a span opened on one line and closed on the next was scoped by nothing at all - corpus two-backticks-are-not-a-code-fence-opening-or-closing is three lines the engine reads as one code span and this grammar read as prose.
patterns.name: markup.raw.inline.carve

patterns.comment: Closed span, like #inline-code: a match rule is line-bounded, so an unclosed opener cannot leak literal scoping into the rest of the document.
patterns.name: markup.raw.inline.literal.carve

patterns.comment: Closed span, like #inline-code: a match rule is line-bounded, so an unclosed opener cannot leak math scoping into the rest of the document. Display ($$) is tried before inline ($).
patterns.name: markup.other.math.display.carve

patterns.comment: CROSS-REFERENCE WITH AUTO TEXT, `</#id>` (grammar.ebnf `auto_text_link`). This file had no rule for it and the run was not left alone: the id begins with `#`, so `#mentions-tags` claimed it and every crossref coloured as a hashtag - the shape markup-carve/tree-sitter-carve#245 found, where a construct parsed as the wrong node made every editor colour a crossref as a web address. It matches at the `<`, two characters before the tag rule can, so it wins on position without reordering anything. The id charset is the spec's `crossref_id` - anything that is not `>`, whitespace or a newline - because an automatic heading id PRESERVES Unicode and case, so `</#Cafe-Notes>` has to scope.
patterns.name: meta.link.cross-reference.carve

patterns.comment: THE PAYLOAD IS LITERAL AND MAY SPAN A LINE BREAK. The spec says nothing inside an editorial comment is parsed as markup and no escape is resolved. This was a single-line `match` whose body also excluded `}`, so `{# a } b #}` was not scoped at all and a comment written across a break coloured the markup inside it - 87 of 286 generated documents (markup-carve/carve-grammars#320). AN ATTRIBUTE BLOCK OPENS THE SAME TWO CHARACTERS: `{#id .c key=value}` is an id plus classes, and a begin of `\\{#` alone claimed it and every line after it. The guard refuses the opener when a `}` NOT preceded by `#` closes on the same line, which is what separates an attribute block from a comment whose closer is `#}`, and leaves a multi-line comment - whose first line holds no `}` at all - opening as it should. A BLANK LINE ENDS IT, which is the bound Prism uses for this construct too. A TextMate begin sees one line and cannot look ahead for its own closer, so without a bound an unclosed opener would scope the rest of the document. One paragraph is where the engine stops reading this construct as well.
patterns.name: comment.block.critic.carve

forced-emphasis.comment: Forced intraword emphasis (spec PART 9 S22): `{*x*}`, `{/x/}`, `{_x_}`, `{~x~}`. Content runs to the closing delimiter, so it may contain the delimiter itself (`{/a/b/}` -> a/b, corpus 01-emphasis-13). These MUST be listed before `#attributes`, because a forced span like `{_path_}` (corpus 01-emphasis-12) is shape-identical to a boolean attribute block and would otherwise be mis-scoped as one.

patterns.comment: THE FIFTH BRACED SPELLING. `{=x=}` is forced HIGHLIGHT (grammar.ebnf `forced_highlight`, spec PART 9 S22), and this context carried the other four and not it. What stood in for it was an accident: the bare `=` rule in `#emphasis` matched the `=x=` INSIDE the braces and left them as prose, which looks right until the content holds the delimiter - `{=a=b=}` scoped nothing at all. Distinct from the raw-inline `{=format}` attribute on a code span, which has no trailing `=` before the `}`.
patterns.name: markup.highlight.carve

patterns.comment: A bare bold run may cross soft line breaks, so this rule carries TextMate state with begin/end. A blank or whitespace-only line ends an unclosed run at its paragraph boundary instead of letting it colour the rest of the file (markup-carve/vscode-carve#178).

patterns.name: markup.highlight.carve
patterns.comment: A BARE `=` THAT BEGINS A SMART-TYPOGRAPHY PATTERN IS NOT AN OPENER (grammar.ebnf, Inline parsing precedence: "a delimiter that begins a multi-char smart-typography pattern: `=>` is the arrow, never a highlight opener - the pattern is consumed first"). Without `(?!>)` the opener `=` of `=>` reached the closer `=` of a later `<=` and scoped the sentence between them as one mark, which is worse than leaving a run uncoloured because the output then claims a construct the document does not hold (carve-grammars#325). THE GUARD BELONGS ON THE OPENER ALONE - once a highlight is open the closer beats the pattern, so `x =y z<= w` marks `y z<` and `x =y z=> w` marks `y z`. It needs no guard against `<`, `>` or `!` BEHIND it: vscode-textmate resolves by POSITION, so on `a <=b c= d` the typography rule starts one column earlier and takes it - and a lookbehind there would refuse `a \!=b c= d`, where the `!` is escaped and the `=` after it is an ordinary opener the engine marks. AN ESCAPED `=` IS NOT A DELIMITER AT ALL (carve-grammars#385): `x =\= y` renders `x == y` with no mark and this rule closed on it. The BODY consumes an escape as a PAIR (`\\.`) and refuses a bare backslash, which settles both directions at once - the escaped `=` is eaten before the closer can see it, and a body that could not hold it would stop there and never reach the real closer past it, so `a =b c\= d= e`, which the engine marks, would have gone from wrongly-coloured to uncoloured. NOT THE UPSTREAM SPELLING WHEN THIS WAS WRITTEN; upstream has since converged on it (markup-carve/carve-grammars#391), so this is now the shared spelling rather than a divergence. carve-grammars counts the backslash run in a lookbehind, `(?<=(?:^|[^\\])(?:\\\\){0,32})` on the closer and its odd-run twin on the body. That is bounded by the repetition it writes out - `{0,32}` counts PAIRS, so a real closer behind 66 backslashes is refused where 64 is still inside, and the odd-run branch on the body fails one step later at 67. This comment used to add that three backslashes were already outside that branch's reach; they are not, and upstream agrees with this grammar on every run up to 64. The three-backslash row is a property of the four bounded lookbehind spellings the IDE's TextMate engine accepts (markup-carve/intellij-carve#117), and was carried across to upstream's spelling by mistake. Consuming the pair has no bound, needs no lookbehind, and reaches the same answer on every row the upstream sweep measures. THREE SHAPES STAY WRONG and are pinned as residuals upstream - `x =<== y`, `x =!== y` and `x =a== y`, a closer followed by another `=`, which the engine marks and `(?![\w=])` refuses; widening that guard means letting the body hold its own delimiter.

A THEMATIC BREAK ON A CONTAINER'S MARKER LINE IS A BREAK, NOT AN EM DASH (markup-carve/vscode-carve#130). `#thematic-break` is `^\\s*(?:-{3,}|\\*{3,}|_{3,})\\s*$`, and on a marker line the container's own begin has already consumed `- ` or `- [ ] ` by the time the line is scanned, so the anchor cannot match and the run of dashes fell through to `#smart-typography`, whose `---` alternative claimed it as `constant.character.typography.carve`. THAT IS WHAT MAKES THIS ONE DIFFERENT from the absent-rule gaps beside it: a scope IS produced, it is the wrong one, and nothing in this repo's invariants looks at whether a produced scope is correct - a presence-only check on the break scope passes the defect unchanged. Corpus 363-a-task-item-s-checkbox-is-not-decided-by-its-first-block renders `- [ ] ---` as an `<hr>` inside the item, and carve-js renders `> ---` as an `<hr>` inside the quote. Anchored on \\G with the `(?<=[ \\t])` guard for the reasons `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` gives, and ordered ahead of `#smart-typography` in both `#container-body` and `#block-quote-body` so the break wins the line. Reachable ONLY from those two, so a document-level `---` after some inline match can never take it. The trailing `[ \\t]*$` keeps it to a whole line: `- --- x` is item text and stays one.
patterns.name: meta.separator.thematic-break.carve

patterns.comment: A COMMENT FENCE MAY OPEN ON A BLOCK-QUOTE MARKER LINE (`> %%%`) too, and the same rule hides its body: spec PART 9 section 24 S2 with section 28 make a comment's body verbatim and invisible WHEREVER the fence sits (corpus 70-blocks-that-render-to-nothing - `> q` / `> %%%` / `> x` / `> %%%` / `> body` renders the quote with `q` and `body` only, markup-carve/vscode-carve#115). tree-sitter-carve is the reference: it puts a fenced_comment_block INSIDE the quote's content, beside the block_quote_marker rather than over it, with the body as a single opaque content node. This grammar INVERTED it - the `%%%` fell through to #trailing-comment and scoped as a LINE comment so no block opened, and the hidden `[r]: /url` came back as a live meta.link.reference.definition.carve on the line below, which is the same failure #113 fixed one marker over. Reached from #block-quotes rather than from #container-body, and NOT by including #comment-fence-on-marker-line: the begin is identical but the end cannot be shared. That rule's closer is INDENTED (`^[ \\t]+`) and its boundary is a column-0 line, and inside a quote both are backwards - the closer carries a `>` marker at column 0 and a column-0 `>` line is the CONTINUATION, not the boundary. Included as-is it closes zero-width on the very next line and hides only the opener. Anchored on \\G for the reason markup-carve/vscode-carve#67 gives for the in-quote reference definition beside it: the quote's own begin has already consumed `> `, so ^ can never match again on that line, and vscode-textmate resets \\G on every following line so this can never open one. The `(?<=[ \\t])` guard keeps it to the marker line - a later match on the same line moves the anchor too, and a percent run glued to the end of one (`> /a/%%%`) is not a fence. Capture 1 is the run of FURTHER markers, so a fence opened at `> > ` is closed at `> > ` and not at `> `; capture 2 is the fence, repeated in the closer so the width matches exactly and `%%%%` does not close `%%%`. The end's second branch is a zero-width quote boundary: an UNMARKED line is where the quote can end, and the engine degrades an unclosed opener to a line comment rather than hiding anything (`> %%%` / `> c` / blank line leaves `c` VISIBLE). Without it an unclosed opener would run to end of document.
patterns.name: comment.block.carve

patterns.comment: A fenced code block inside a quote needs a quote-aware region. A normal multi-line fence child would prevent the enclosing one-line quote rule from ending, so this rule repeats the quote prefix in its closer and stops at the first unmarked line.
patterns.name: markup.raw.block.fenced.code.carve

patterns.comment:
A COMMENT FENCE MAY OPEN ON A LIST ITEM'S MARKER LINE (`- %%%`), and then its body is hidden exactly as it is anywhere else: spec PART 9 section 24 S2 with section 28 make a comment's body verbatim and invisible WHEREVER the fence sits, so the whole run from opener to closer is one comment and nothing after it is affected (corpus 337-a-comment-fence-opened-on-an-item-s-marker-line-hides-its-body-too, markup-carve/vscode-carve#113). The `#comments` fence cannot reach that shape: its begin is anchored on ^, and the container's own begin match has already consumed `- ` by the time this line is scanned. The result was INVERTED highlighting - the `%%%` fell through to the trailing-comment rule and scoped as a LINE comment so no block opened, the hidden `[r]: /url` came back as a live meta.link.reference.definition.carve, and the REAL closer was then taken for an opener and swallowed the paragraph below. tree-sitter-carve is the reference here (all three carve-grammars highlighters were wrong, each differently): it puts a fenced_comment_block INSIDE list_item_content, beside the list_marker_* rather than over it, with the body as a single opaque content node. Anchored on \G rather than ^ for the reason markup-carve/vscode-carve#67 gives for the in-quote reference definition - \G matches at the current scan position, which on a marker line is exactly where the marker ended, and which vscode-textmate resets on every following line so this can never open one. The `(?<=[ \t])` guard is what keeps it to a marker line specifically: a later match on the same line moves the \G anchor too, and a `%%%` run glued to the end of one (`- /a/%%%`) is not a fence. The end has TWO branches. The first is the ordinary closer, INDENTED because the closer sits at the item's content column. The second is a zero-width container boundary: a column-0 line ends the item and with it the open fence, so corpus 326-a-column-0-line-after-a-container-s-last-block-when-that-block-left-no-paragraph-open-6 (`- %%%` / `c` / `%%%` / `tail`) keeps `c` and `tail` VISIBLE with the unclosed opener degrading to a line comment. Without it an unclosed opener would run to end of document, which is the failure this rule exists to remove. A NESTED MARKER LINE NEVER REACHES COLUMN 0, so that boundary could not fire for one, and a fence opened at ` - %%%` swallowed its own sibling ` - sibling` (markup-carve/vscode-carve#127). The enclosing `#list_item` does not save it: vscode-textmate only tests the CURRENT rule's `end` alongside its patterns, so an enclosing container's `end` is never reached while the fence is open. THE BEGIN THEREFORE HAS A SECOND BRANCH that matches a nested marker line WHOLE, which is the only way this rule can learn the opener's indent - the \G branch starts after the container's own begin match, captures nothing before it, and Oniguruma has no variable-length lookbehind to recover it with. The two branches then share one `end`: capture 1 is the opener's indent, and vscode-textmate splices an unset capture as the empty string, so on the \G branch `^(?![ \t]*$)(?!\1[ \t])` degrades to exactly the column-0 boundary this rule had before. THE BLANK-LINE GUARD IS PART OF THAT EQUIVALENCE and not decoration: an item spans blank lines and so does a fence inside it, so `- %%%` over a blank line over ` hidden` over ` %%%` hides `hidden` (carve-js renders `
`). Without the guard the boundary fires on the blank line, `hidden` comes back visible, and the real closer is then read as an opener that swallows the paragraph below - the same inversion markup-carve/vscode-carve#113 removed. markup-carve/intellij-carve#74 closed the same gap with `^(?!\1[ \t])` and could use it unconditionally because its rule always matches the marker line whole; here that shape is the fallback, not the rule. THE COST of the second branch is that the marker it consumes sits inside `comment.block.carve` rather than beside it, which is not tree-sitter-carve's split - the capture patterns put the list scopes back on top so a theme still colours the marker as a marker, and the \G branch, which is every column-0 spelling, is unaffected. The boundary the second branch produces is the opener's indent PLUS ONE COLUMN rather than the item's exact content column, for the same reason the glued-attribute list branches use a minimum column: it holds the comment open a column or two too long rather than closing it early.
patterns.name: comment.block.carve

container-body.comment: The pattern set a container's body reaches, shared by every rule that opens one so they cannot drift apart. It is the top-level list minus `#frontmatter`, which is document-start only, with `#definitions-in-container` standing in for `#definitions`: a definition is flush-left at document level and indented here, and the container's `end` has already established that an indented line inside it sits at or beyond the container's content column. `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` leads, and is reachable ONLY from here: it is the one rule that has to fire mid-line, on the container's own opening line.

definitions-in-container.comment: Definitions reachable only from a container's body. The container's `end` has already established that the line sits at or beyond its content column, which a line-anchored whitespace run cannot know on its own.

patterns.comment: An abbreviation definition at a container's content column must be consumed before the inline layer can mistake its leading star for bold (markup-carve/vscode-carve#179).
patterns.name: meta.abbreviation.definition.carve

hard-break.comment: A trailing backslash is a HARD BREAK, and it survives into the rendered line - the line block cases keep it (corpus a-line-block-s-hard-break-keeps-its-backslash and a-line-block-s-last-body-line-keeps-its-backslash). carve-grammars and the intellij-carve bundle have both scoped it as constant.character.escape.hard-break.carve since before this port; this grammar had no rule for it at all, so the backslash tokenized as ordinary text. Same match and same scope as those two on purpose: a third spelling of one production is how the three grammars drift.

block-quote-body.comment: The pattern set a block quote's own line reaches, shared by `#block-quotes` and `#block-quote-on-marker-line` so the two cannot drift apart - the same reason `#container-body` exists for containers. Both rules differ only in their anchor: one opens at the line start, the other at the scan position on a list item's marker line.

patterns.comment: A link/footnote reference definition is collected wherever its container puts it (markup-carve/carve#660), so it is recognized inside a quote too - unlike an abbreviation definition, which stays document-level-only (markup-carve/carve#611) and is deliberately NOT duplicated here. Anchored on \G rather than ^: the quote's own begin match has already consumed the `> ` prefix, so ^ (true column 0 of the line) can never match again on the same line - \G matches at the current scan position instead (markup-carve/vscode-carve#67).
patterns.name: meta.link.reference.definition.carve

patterns.comment:
A BLOCK QUOTE MAY OPEN ON A LIST ITEM'S OWN MARKER LINE (`- > x`, `1. > x`, `- - > x`, `- [ ] > x`), and it takes the rest of that line: carve-js at the pinned engine renders `

  • x

`. `#block-quotes` cannot reach it - its begin is anchored on ^, and the container's own begin match has already consumed the marker by the time this line is scanned - so the whole line fell through to the list rule and everything after the marker carried NO scope at all, while `- > %%%` inverted the same way `#113` and `#115` describe: the `%%%` scoped as a trailing LINE comment so no block opened, and the hidden `[r]: /url` came back live (markup-carve/vscode-carve#125). Anchored on \G with the `(?<=[ \t])` guard for the reasons `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` gives: \G matches at the current scan position, which on a marker line is where the marker ended, vscode-textmate resets it on every following line so this can never open one, and the guard keeps it to a marker line rather than to a `>` glued after some earlier match. Reachable ONLY from `#container-body`, so a document-level line can never take it. The marker keeps its own quote punctuation scope, which is tree-sitter-carve's split (markup-carve/tree-sitter-carve#218): the `block_quote` sits inside `list_item_content` beside the `list_marker_*` rather than over it.
